### Watercolour (`lumenary:watercolour`, models this process)

_From: European and East Asian painting; when: Centuries old, English school of the 18th and 19th centuries; works best on: Landscapes, flowers and soft portraits._

Watercolour is thin pigment carried by water, so the white of the paper shows through it and a stroke can only ever darken what lies beneath. That one fact explains the whole look: bright areas are simply left unpainted, colours bleed into one another, and pigment pools in dark rims where a wash dried. This treatment works in pigment laid over a paper colour for exactly that reason.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Blur the picture by an amount set by the bleed slider to stand in for water spreading.
2. Read it from slightly displaced places, nudged by slow noise, for the wobble of a wet brush.
3. Pull each channel part way toward the nearest of seven levels, because washes settle in flat tonal steps.
4. Compute pigment as darkness times small effects: nothing in the lightest areas, uneven blooms from broad noise, granulation from fine noise, and pooling at edges.
5. Darken the paper with that pigment, then add an optional unpainted border and a faint fibre pattern.

**The maths:**

$$\tilde v=v+0.55\left(\frac{\operatorname{round}(7v)}{7}-v\right)$$

_Each channel v (0 to 1) of the blurred picture is flattened toward seven levels._ (primitives: tone-bands)

$$m=\operatorname{clip}\Big[(1-\tilde v)\;s\;\ell\;b\;g\;\big(1+1.1\,\rho\,e\big)\Big]$$

_s is the colour strength (0.45 to 1.2), ℓ = 1 − smoothstep(0.8, 0.97, L) the lift that keeps highlights bare, b bloom, g granulation, ρ the rim slider and e = smoothstep(0.015, 0.09, edge strength) the pooling at edges._ (primitives: soft-threshold, image-gradient)

$$C=C_{\text{paper}}\,\big(1-0.94\,m\big)$$

_The pigment only darkens the paper beneath it, channel by channel._ (primitives: multiply-blend)

**Dials:** `bleed` (Bleed) = 50 [0 to 100]; `wash` (Colour strength) = 70 [20 to 100]; `rim` (Dark rims) = 55 [0 to 100]; `grain` (Paper grain) = 50 [0 to 100]; `paper` (Paper) = "cream" (cream, white, rough); `margin` (Unpainted border) = true; `seed` (New washes) = 1.

**History:** Painting with water-based colour is ancient, but the English school of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with artists such as Thomas Girtin and J. M. W. Turner, made it a major art of landscape. Albrecht Dürer had already painted detailed watercolour studies of plants and animals around 1500. Portable paint boxes later put watercolour in the hands of travellers and amateurs.
